brief: Ten cents a chip means the cheapest possible bench for register-level experiments on real RISC-V silicon: 48MHz RV32, 2KB SRAM, 16KB flash. A $6.90 dev board is already on Tindie. If you want a throwaway target for bare-metal bring-up practice, there is no cheaper seat.
title: WCH launches a sub-10 cent RISC-V microcontroller, and a $6.90 dev board is already here

brief: The V4.0 Mi-V soft-core adds Hamming-coded state machines, triple-modular-redundant registers, and ECC RAM options for PolarFire FPGAs. The safety techniques are the real story: Hamming-encoded FSMs and triplicated registers are patterns you can lift into your own RTL, and this is a working checklist for any safety-adjacent FPGA design.
title: Microchip upgrades its Mi-V RV32 soft-core, promises a major speed boost

brief: A compact walk through the three embedded extensions that matter most: C (compressed, 15 to 30 percent smaller code), E (16 registers for tiny MCUs), and M (hardware multiply and divide). If you are picking a core for a constrained board, this is the ten-minute version of the decision you will actually make.
title: RISC-V extensions for high performance embedded computing

brief: Ten hours of kernel debugging brought an AMD RX 6700XT up on a HiFive Unmatched, with hardware-accelerated rendering and VAAPI encode. Desktop-class PCIe bring-up on RISC-V is no longer theory. The patch is the artifact: read it for how a real bring-up debugger narrows a driver problem on unfamiliar silicon.
title: Rene Rebe patches the Linux kernel for a first look at a Radeon RX 6700XT on a RISC-V PC

brief: 2026 is being called the year of RVA silicon: up to 128-core server parts, and vector plus matrix extensions running control software and ML on the same core instead of a separate NPU. Read it as a map of where the ecosystem's engineering hours are going, not as a buying guide.
title: RISC-V Europe Summit 2026: beyond embedded electronics

brief: M-mode boot, M to S to U transitions, trap delegation, a 140-byte trap frame, and every feature verified in GDB before commit. Reads like a study companion to the xv6 trap chapters, except every claim was checked in a debugger. The trap-frame layout and the GDB workflow are the parts worth stealing.
title: kore: a minimal RISC-V operating system built from scratch on RV32I

brief: Rust in the kernel leaves the experimental phase and becomes officially supported, in the same release that strengthens RISC-V support. If you write kernel code, the Rust question is now settled policy rather than an experiment. Track the tree, not the announcement.
title: Linux 7.0 released with official Rust support

brief: Configurable PMP granularity, control-flow-integrity fixes, and timer and MMU correctness fixes for RISC-V. This is the emulator that trap and memory experiments get verified against, so its changelog doubles as a to-read list of behaviors your own tests should cover.
title: QEMU 10.2 expands RISC-V emulation capabilities

brief: Charlie Jenkins's RFC series adds a RISCV_ISA_RVA23 Kconfig target, the ZVE23X vector subset, and extension-aware compiler flags to the kernel build. This is what it looks like when a hardware profile becomes a build target. Read the series before writing any code that assumes RVA23.
title: New patches lay out Linux kernel adjustments for RISC-V RVA23 hardware

brief: A field SOP for getting firmware off a device: triple-read every flash dump with flashrom and compare hashes, probe UART at 115200 8N1, drive JTAG through OpenOCD with concrete commands. The habit that matters is the triple read and hash compare, cheap insurance against a flaky clip corrupting your only copy.
title: Firmware reverse engineering SOP: acquisition, extraction, analysis
